The three columns

  • Arrives — scheduled stop. Delays push it, plans don't.
  • Calling at — the stations between. Match your stop exactly.

Some timetables mark departure as d and arrival as a. Same thing, shorter ink.

Anatomy of one row

Beware the platform change. The board updates before the timetable does — trust the board at the station.

What the little footnotes mean
  • SX — runs on Saturdays only.
  • M — Mondays only.
  • 1st — first class carriages only at that stop.

Footnotes apply to the specific column they sit above, not the whole row.

Peak vs off-peak

Peak fares usually start around 06:30 and end around 09:30, then return for the evening. Off-peak tickets bought for peak trains get you a fine, user_name. Check the operator, not just the clock.

Replacing a watch battery

Most quartz watches pop open easily, user_name>. The trick is patience and the right size cell — not brute force.

You'll need

  • A case-back knife or a small flat-head screwdriver
  • Finger cots or tape (the movement hates fingerprints)
  • A fresh cell — check the old one for the number (usually CR2016 or CR2032)
  • A soft cloth and a toothpick

If it's a diving watch or has a screw-down back, stop and take it to someone with a press. Waterproofing depends on that gasket.

Battery cells at a glance

The number is diameter / thickness in millimetres. Bigger last number, thicker cell.

Step by step
  1. Set the watch face-down on a cloth so you can see the back hatch.
  2. Find the tiny lip near the notch. Slide the blade under and twist gently.
  3. Lift the back off. Snap a photo if springs fly out.
  4. Use the toothpick to ease the old cell out from the edge.
  5. Press the new cell in with the plus side facing up.
  6. Check it ticks. Then reseat the gasket and press the back until it clicks.
It still won't run

If the hands don't move, the issue isn't the cell — the movement may need a clean, or the crown is pulled out to a setting position. Push the crown all the way in and try again.

Sleep is mostly a timing problem, user_name>, not a willpower one. Get the rhythm right and the rest follows.

The four levers

  • Light — bright morning, dim evening. Your body reads light as the clock.
  • Temperature — a cool room helps you drop off. Around 17–19°C works for most.
  • Timing — same wake-up time every day, weekends included.
  • Pressure — if you're awake 20 minutes, get up and read somewhere dim.

Sleep pressure through the day

The line is drowsiness. Naps take a bite out of it; caffeine hides it.

Waking at 3am, wide awake

Common and annoying. Usually a dip in the sleep cycle, a warm room, or a drink too close to bed. Don't check the clock — that teaches your brain to be alert at 3am. Stay still and dim.

The bedtime wind-down
  1. One hour before bed, dull the lights.
  2. Put the phone across the room on charge.
  3. Warm shower if you like — the drop in body temperature after helps.
  4. Read something on paper until your eyelids argue.

Do this three nights in a row and your body starts expecting sleep at the same time. Boring, but it works.

Making a fire without matches

Sparks need something to land on, user_name>. Build the tinder bundle first and the fire part is easy.

The three-size rule

  • Tinder — dry grass, birch bark, char cloth, cotton. Must catch from a spark.
  • Kindling — pencil-thick dry twigs.
  • Fuel — wrist-thick and up, dry deadwood.

Damp wood steals heat, no matter how good your spark. If it snaps easily, it's dry enough.

Lay the tinder bundle

Tepee lay pulls air up through the middle. Best for a quick start.

Using a ferro rod
  1. Anchor the rod close to the tinder.
  2. Draw the striker down the rod with firm, long strokes — don't flick at it.
  3. Catch the sparks on char cloth or dry pith.
  4. Fold the tinder around the ember and blow gently, steadily, from below.
If it goes out

Feed small, then bigger. Smothering a young flame with big logs is the classic mistake. Give it air and patience, and don't rearrange everything at once.

Cutting onions without tears

It's the root, user_name>. Leave it attached and the fumes have less to work with.

The physics of the sting

Sliced cells release a sulfur compound. It meets moisture in your eyes, turns into a mild acid, and your eyes flood to flush it out.

So: cut fewer cells at once, slow the reaction, or keep the gas out of your eyes.

What actually helps

  • Chill the onion 15 minutes first
  • Cut near a running tap or an open window
  • Keep the root end intact until the end
  • Breathe through your mouth, not your nose

Myth: rubbing your eyes after makes it better. It does not. Wash your hands first.

The dice in four moves
  1. Halve it from stem to root.
  2. Peel, then make horizontal cuts towards the root.
  3. Make vertical cuts parallel to the root.
  4. Slice across and the dice fall out on their own.
If you really hate it

Buy frozen diced onion. Two minutes saved, zero tears. No shame, user_name>.

instances.html:
Changing a lightbulb safely

Boring job, real hazards, user_name>. Two minutes of care beats a burned hand or a broken fitting.

Before you touch it

  • Switch the light off at the wall, not just the pull cord.
  • Let a hot bulb cool for five minutes — halogen can burn you fast.
  • Use a ladder that's level, not a chair. Chairs wobble.

If the fitting is cracked or the bulb is stuck, stop. Forcing a stuck bayonet bulb can shatter glass in your hand.

Two common bases

Push and twist for bayonet. Turn like a jar lid for screw.

What wattage to buy

Never exceed the wattage printed inside the fitting. LEDs run cooler and use far less power, so a 9W LED can often replace a 60W old-style bulb and stay well inside the limit.

Bayonet still won't shift
  1. Press in firmly first, then push and twist.
  2. Wear a glove or grip it with a dry cloth.
  3. If it's really seized, cut the power and leave it for someone with a proper remover.

Cleaning a dishwasher

Because it's washing dishes, not itself. Five minutes a month keeps it sweet.

The monthly reset

  1. Pull the bottom rack out.
  2. Unscrew the filter — it's the cylindrical thing at the back. Rinse under hot water.
  3. Scrub the door seal with a soapy sponge. Gunk loves that crevice.
  4. Run a hot cycle with a cup of white vinegar in the top rack.

Skip the vinegar if your manual says so — some seals don't like acid. A dishwasher tablet works too.

Smell check

If it still smells after a clean, run an empty cycle with a scoop of baking soda on the bottom. Then leave the door ajar between uses.

Time 5min

Getting rid of fruit flies

They're not evil, just enthusiastic. Break the cycle and they'll thin out in a few days.

The trap

  1. Put a splash of apple cider vinegar in a small bowl.
  2. Add a drop of dish soap — it breaks the surface tension.
  3. Cover with cling film and poke a few holes.
  4. Leave it near the fruit bowl. Empty daily.

Prevention

  • Rinse cans and bottles before recycling.
  • Keep fruit in the fridge if you can.
  • Take out the compost caddy every night.
  • Check the drain — they breed in gunky pipes too.

Most infestations clear in 3–5 days once the source is gone.

Ironing a shirt

Low heat, steady strokes, and a little patience. Your collar will thank you.

Order of operations

  1. Collar first — press from the points inward.
  2. Cuffs, then sleeves. Iron towards the shoulder.
  3. Body: start at the back, then front panels.
  4. Hang immediately to let it cool flat.

Heat cheat sheet

  • Cotton: high heat, steam on.
  • Poly blend: medium, no steam.
  • Linen: high, iron damp.
  • Silk: low, use a cloth.

Never iron over buttons or zips — they'll scratch the plate and crack.

Storing fresh herbs

Treat them like cut flowers or salad leaves — depends on the herb.

Soft herbs (basil, cilantro, parsley)

Trim the stems, stand them in a glass with an inch of water. Cover loosely with a plastic bag and leave on the counter. Basil hates the cold.

Hard herbs (rosemary, thyme, sage)

Wrap in a slightly damp paper towel, then a bag, and refrigerate. They'll keep for a week or two.

Freeze leftovers in olive oil in an ice cube tray. Instant flavour bombs.

Fixing a stuck zipper

Nine times out of ten it's a grain of grit or a bent tooth. You can usually save it.

If it's stuck

  1. Don't yank. Hold the fabric flat.
  2. Rub a graphite pencil along the teeth.
  3. Or apply a little lip balm or soap.
  4. Work the slider gently back and forth.

If it splits open

The slider is probably bent. Squeeze it gently with pliers — barely any pressure. If that fails, a new slider is a cheap fix at a tailor.

For plastic zippers, a dab of silicone grease works wonders.

Cleaning a coffee grinder

Old oils go rancid and make every cup taste like yesterday. A quick clean fixes it.

Quick clean (weekly)

  1. Unplug it.
  2. Grind a handful of dry white rice until powdery.
  3. Dump the rice and brush out the chamber.
  4. Wipe the burrs with a dry cloth.

Deep clean (monthly)

Unscrew the top burr if your model allows. Brush with a stiff brush. Never rinse with water — moisture kills grinders.

Don't use rice if you have a high-end conical burr grinder; it can wear the burrs. Use grinder cleaning pellets instead.

Smoke Detector Testing

Quick check: press and hold the test button. If it doesn't chirp, it's not protecting you.

Test it

  • Press and hold the test button for a few seconds.
  • You should hear a loud, piercing alarm.
  • If it's weak or silent, replace the battery or the unit.

Monthly routine

  1. Test every month.
  2. Vacuum the vents gently.
  3. Replace batteries yearly (or when chirping).
  4. Replace the whole unit every 10 years.

Nuisance alarms? Move it away from the kitchen or bathroom, or buy a photoelectric model.

Not sure what kind you have? Look for the label on the back.

Budgeting Basics

A budget is just a plan for your money. You don't need a fancy app to start.

Track it

For one month, write down every expense. Use a notes app, a spreadsheet, or a notebook. The goal is awareness, not perfection.

Sort it

Group spending into needs (rent, food), wants (streaming, dining out), and savings. Aim for 50/30/20 as a rough guide.

Tip: Automate savings first. Even $20 a week adds up.

Review your budget monthly. Life changes, and so should your plan.

Cleaning a Washing Machine

That musty smell? It's mildew. Here's how to evict it.

Run a hot cycle

  1. Add 2 cups of white vinegar to the drum.
  2. Run an empty hot water cycle.
  3. Wipe the door seal and detergent drawer.

Monthly upkeep

  • Leave the door ajar between loads.
  • Use less detergent (excess feeds mildew).
  • Clean the filter if you have one.

Don't mix vinegar and bleach. It creates toxic gas. Use one or the other.

Front-loaders need this more often than top-loaders.

Tying a Tie

The four-in-hand is the easiest knot. Once you know it, you'll never forget.

Steps

  1. Drape the tie around your neck, seam side down. Wide end on your right, about a foot lower.
  2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end.
  3. Bring the wide end up through the loop around your neck.
  4. Wrap it across the front of the knot.
  5. Pull it up through the loop again.
  6. Slide the knot up and tighten.

Tips

  • The knot should sit at your collar, not below it.
  • The tie's tip should reach your belt buckle.
  • Dimple the knot with a pinch before tightening.

Windsor knot? Same idea, but wrap the wide end around twice before pulling through.

Practice on your thigh first. Seriously.

Removing a Stripped Screw

When the screwdriver just spins, try these tricks before you drill.

Try this first

  • Use a rubber band: place it between the screw head and driver for grip.
  • Switch to a larger flathead or a star bit that bites.
  • Apply downward pressure while turning slowly.

If that fails

  • Use a screw extractor kit.
  • Carefully cut a new slot with a rotary tool.
  • Drill off the head, then remove the shaft with pliers.

Be patient. Rushing can damage the surrounding material.

A drop of penetrating oil can help if the screw is rusted.

Fixing a Squeaky Floor

Squeaks come from movement between wood and nails. Silence it from above or below.

From above

  • Locate the squeak by walking slowly.
  • Drive a trim-head screw through the carpet or wood into the joist.
  • Countersink and fill the hole.

From below

  • If you have access, insert a shim coated in wood glue between the subfloor and joist.
  • Tap it in gently, then snap off the excess.

Tip: A little talcum powder in the gap can quiet minor squeaks temporarily.

Find the exact spot by having someone walk while you listen below.

Folding a fitted sheet

You don't need the corners to meet. You need the elastic to hide.

Four moves, no tears

  1. Hold it inside-out, hands in two corners.
  2. Fold corner over corner, tucking one into the other.
  3. Lay flat, elastic bunched to one end.
  4. Fold in thirds, then crosswise.

Shelf life: about a week before the pile collapses anyway.

Where the pain lives

Corners and elastic cause most of the swearing, user_name.

The absurdly fast version

Fold the whole thing in half twice, then stuff it in the pillowcase with its sheet-mate. Nobody sees the cupboard.

Reading a measuring tape

Tiny ticks, loud opinions. Here's the shorthand.

The tick ladder

  • Longest line = whole inch.
  • Half, then quarter, then eighth.
  • Sixteenth = shortest marks.
  • Boxed numbers every 12 in = feet.
  • Red dot every 16 in = stud spacing.

Half-inch feel

Halfway between two long marks. That's it. That's the secret.

Hook the metal tab over the edge and pull. It slides a little on purpose.

What's the slot in the end for?

It hooks onto a nail head so you can measure solo. Also lets the hook shift for inside vs outside measuring, user_name.

Building a campfire in the rain

Dry wood is the whole trick. Find it, hide it, then burn it.

Find the dry

  • Dead branches still on the tree.
  • Under dense evergreens.
  • Split a log: the middle stayed dry.
  • Pine resin, birch bark, dead grass.
  • Your own pocket lint. Genuinely.

Wet-to-lit odds

Get the tinder lit and the rest forgives you.

Keep it alive

Shield with your body, stack small fuel over big, and don't smother it. Rain on a hot bed of coals is fine, user_name.

Sharpening a kitchen knife

Ten minutes on a stone beats a year of wishful honing.

Two jobs, don't mix them

  • Hone weekly: realigns the edge.
  • Sharpen rarely: removes steel.
  • Angle: about 15–20° per side.
  • Count strokes, keep them even.
  • Finish with light passes on each side.

Edge after each step

Honing steel

Whetstone

The paper test: a sharp knife glides through printer paper without tearing.

No stone at home?

A coffee mug's unglazed base works in a pinch. Twenty light strokes per side, user_name.

Making cheap coffee taste better

Cheap beans aren't the problem. Grind, ratio and water usually are.

Cheap fixes, ranked

  1. Grind fresh, just before brewing.
  2. Weigh it: about 1:16 coffee to water.
  3. Use filtered or bottled water.
  4. Brew hot but not boiling.
  5. Clean the machine. Old oils ruin everything.

What each fix buys you

Freshly ground does the heavy lifting, user_name.

Bean storage

Airtight, cool, dark, and away from the kettle steam. Freezer's fine if sealed properly; fridge is not.
